## Define \alert{random trial}

- What's going to happen tomorrow?
- If I flip a coin---heads or tails?
- If I roll a die, what number comes up?
- If I measure a fish, how long is it?
- If I conduct an insect survey in the Koʻolau Mountains, how many species will I find?
- What is the effect of a new drug on a patient enrolled in a clinical trial?

These are all \alert{random trials}


## Define \alert{random trial}

\it A \alert{random trial} is a process or experiment that has two or more possible outcomes whose occurrence cannot be predicted with certainty


![](../../img/die_roll.png)


## Define \alert{event} and \alert{outcome}

\it An \alert{event} is one observation of a random trial

\it The \alert{outcomes} of a random trial describe all the possible events


## Define \alert{random trial}, \alert{event}, and \alert{outcome} {.t}

## Define \alert{probability}

\it The \alert{probability} of an event is the proportion of times that event would occur if we repeated a random trial over and over again under the same conditions. Probability *always* ranges between 0 and 1



## Define \alert{probability}

With a fair die, every outcome has equal probability:

```{r}
library(tidydice)
library(gridExtra)


d1 <- roll_dice(times = 1, prob = c(1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0)) |>
    plot_dice(detailed = FALSE) + labs(title = NULL)
d2 <- roll_dice(times = 1, prob = c(0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0)) |>
    plot_dice(detailed = FALSE) + labs(title = NULL)
d3 <- roll_dice(times = 1, prob = c(0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0)) |>
    plot_dice(detailed = FALSE) + labs(title = NULL)
d4 <- roll_dice(times = 1, prob = c(0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0)) |>
    plot_dice(detailed = FALSE) + labs(title = NULL)
d5 <- roll_dice(times = 1, prob = c(0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0)) |>
    plot_dice(detailed = FALSE) + labs(title = NULL)
d6 <- roll_dice(times = 1, prob = c(0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1), success = 1) |>
    plot_dice(detailed = FALSE) + labs(title = NULL)


pr <- data.frame(rep("= 1/6", 6))
names(pr) <- NULL
rownames(pr) <- paste0("Pr(rolling a ", 1:6, ")")

grid.arrange(d1, tableGrob(pr[1, ], theme = ttheme_default(base_size = 32)),
             d2, tableGrob(pr[2, ], theme = ttheme_default(base_size = 32)),
             d3, tableGrob(pr[3, ], theme = ttheme_default(base_size = 32)),
             d4, tableGrob(pr[4, ], theme = ttheme_default(base_size = 32)),
             d5, tableGrob(pr[5, ], theme = ttheme_default(base_size = 32)),
             d6, tableGrob(pr[6, ], theme = ttheme_default(base_size = 32)),
             ncol = 2)

```


## Define \alert{probability}

Probability is just counting, sometimes *very complex* counting.

But with a die it is simple counting:

$Pr(rolling~a~5) = 1/6$

because there is only **1** way to roll a 5, and there are **6** possible outcomes

Probability is all the ways you could get a specific event, divided by the number of possible outcomes


## Define \alert{probability}

Probability is all the ways you could get a specific event, divided by the number of possible outcomes

Consider rolling **2 dice** what are all the possible outcomes?

\begin{alertblock}{Pause \& Think}
  Why is 7 a lucky number in many cultures?
\end{alertblock}


## Define \alert{probability}

Probability is all the ways you could get a specific event, divided by the number of possible outcomes

\small
```{r eval = FALSE, echo = TRUE}
# all the ways to get 7 from 2 dice:
# (1, 6); (6, 1); (2, 5); (5, 2)
# (3, 4); (4, 3)
6

# number of possible outcomes of 2 dice:
6 * 6

# probability of rolling a 7:
6 / 36 # = 1/6
```


## Define \alert{probability}

Probability is all the ways you could get a specific event, divided by the number of possible outcomes

\small
```{r echo = TRUE, eval = FALSE}
# simulate it
nroll <- 10000
crap <- replicate(nroll, {
    d1 <- sample(6, 1)
    d2 <- sample(6, 1)
    
    d1 + d2
})

sum(crap == 7) / nroll # this should be about 1/6
```

## Define \alert{probability}

Probability is all the ways you could get a specific event, divided by the number of possible outcomes

\small
```{r echo = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
# simulate it
nroll <- 10000
crap <- replicate(nroll, {
    d1 <- sample(6, 1)
    d2 <- sample(6, 1)
    
    d1 + d2
})
```

Instead of looking at one probability:

```{r echo = TRUE, eval = FALSE}
sum(crap == 7) / nroll # this should be about 1/6
```


## Define \alert{probability distribution}

We could make a histogram-looking thing of all probabilities:
\vspace{2em}

```{r dicedist, echo = FALSE, eval = TRUE, fig.width=4, fig.height=2, cache=TRUE}
ggplot(data.frame(sum_of_2_dice = crap), aes(x = sum_of_2_dice)) +
    geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), 
                   binwidth = 1, color = "black") + 
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2, 12, by = 1)) +
    theme_cowplot()
```

This histogram-looking thing is called a \alert{probability distribution}

## Define \alert{probability distribution}

![](../../img/2_dice_hist.png)

This histogram-looking thing is called a \alert{discrete probability distribution}

## Why do we care?

Probability is everywhere!

*If I conduct an insect survey, how many species will I find?* What are all the outcomes:

\begin{tabular}{p{7cm} l}
Process & Event \\
\hline
No populations establish & $S = 0$ \\
A population establishes and goes extinct & $S = 0$ \\
2 population establish and 1 goes extinct & $S = 1$ \\
$\cdots$ & $\cdots$ \\
N populations establish, M go extinct & $S = N - M$ \\
$\cdots$ & $\cdots$ \\
N populations establish, none go extinct & $S = N$ \\
$\cdots$ & $\cdots$
\end{tabular}

\LARGE
*Complex counting!*

## Why do we care?


::: columns

:::: column

*Remember noni?*
  
Suppose we run a clinical study of the effect of noni juice on inflammatory arthritis. We randomly assign half the patients to receive 10mg noni extract and the other half to receive a placebo. We measure change in erythrocyte sedimentation rate (*sed rate*) in all patients before and after treatment (either 10mg noni or placebo)

::::

:::: column

```{r, fig.width=3, fig.height=4}
set.seed(1)
dat <- data.frame(sed = c(rnorm(100, -2), rnorm(100)), 
                  group = c(rep("10mg noni", 100), 
                            rep("placebo", 100)))

ggplot(dat, aes(x = sed, fill = group)) +
    geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 20) +
    facet_grid(rows = vars(group)) +
    theme_cowplot() +
    theme(legend.position = "none") +
    xlab("Change in sed rate [mm/hr]\n(after - before)")

```

::::

:::

## Define \alert{continuous probability distribution}

```{r sedhist, echo = FALSE, eval = TRUE, fig.width=4, fig.height=2, cache=TRUE}
ggplot(dat[dat$group != "placebo", ], aes(x = sed, fill = group)) +
    geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 20) +
    facet_grid(rows = vars(group)) +
    theme_cowplot() +
    theme(legend.position = "none") +
    xlab("Change in sed rate [mm/hr]\n(after - before)")
```

*Change in sed rate [mm/hr] is* **not** *an integer*

\LARGE What do we do?!


## Define \alert{continuous probability distribution}

![](../../img/sed_hist.png)


## Define \alert{continuous probability distribution}

Imagine we had millions of data points, and we could draw very narrow bins

```{r echo = FALSE, eval = TRUE, fig.width=4, fig.height=2}
dat <- data.frame(sed = rnorm(1000000, -2), group = "10mg noni")

ggplot(dat, aes(x = sed, fill = group)) +
    geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 100) +
    facet_grid(rows = vars(group)) +
    theme_cowplot() +
    theme(legend.position = "none") +
    xlab("Change in sed rate [mm/hr]\n(after - before)")
```

We would get a very smooth looking distribution

## Define \alert{continuous probability distribution}

Continuous probability distributions are typically visualized as smooth curves, *without bars*

```{r seddens, echo = FALSE, eval = TRUE, fig.width=4, fig.height=2, cache=TRUE}
ggplot(dat, aes(x = sed, fill = group)) +
    geom_density() +
    facet_grid(rows = vars(group)) +
    theme_cowplot() +
    theme(legend.position = "none") +
    xlab("Change in sed rate [mm/hr]\n(after - before)")
```


## Define \alert{continuous probability distribution}

Continuous probability distributions are typically visualized as smooth curves, *without bars*

```{r, eval = FALSE, echo = FALSE}
rich <- replicate(1000, {
    nspp <- 500
    mus <- rgamma(nspp, 10, 0.1)
    ks <- rexp(nspp, 10)
    
    ps <- 1 - dnbinom(0, mu = mus, size = ks)
    # sum(ps >= runif(nspp))
    sum(rbinom(nspp, 1, ps * runif(nspp, min = 0.1)))
})

hist(rich)
```
